Memo
Subject: Scheduling challenge and approach for the multi‑mode, resource‑constrained project

Overview
We are preparing a detailed delivery schedule for a project that includes multiple interdependent activities, each of which can be executed in more than one way. The work draws on shared, limited-capacity resources and must be delivered within a firm spending cap. Our task is to select how each activity will be executed and to determine start times that respect all timing, resource, and budget constraints while shortening overall completion as much as possible.

Execution options and trade‑offs
- Each activity must be executed in exactly one mode. Each mode specifies a different duration, resource usage profile, and direct execution cost.
- Faster modes accelerate delivery but are more expensive; slower modes are less costly and may consume fewer resources.
- Activities, once started, run to completion without interruption (no preemption).
- All resources are renewable: when an activity completes, the resources it used become available for other work.

Dependencies and timing rules
- Precedence links define the order of execution. Some successors must wait at least a stated minimum time after their predecessors finish (minimum delay rules).
- A subset of dependencies also limit how long we can wait: certain successors must start within a stated maximum time after the predecessor’s finish (maximum delay rules).
- Several activities have earliest allowed start times (release dates) and some have fixed completion deadlines.

Resource conflict policy
- We are applying a conservative safety rule for activities that are not connected by a precedence link. If there exists even one combination of modes—one mode for each activity—and at least one resource for which their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities may not overlap. In that case, the schedule must sequence them so one finishes before the other starts.
- This pairwise safety rule is the only resource constraint. There is no separate, continuous “capacity at all times” check beyond the sequencing commitments implied by this rule.
- The implication is that even if some mode pairings would fit concurrently, the potential for an overload in any other pairing requires us to choose an order to avoid risk.

Budget guardrail
- The sum of the direct execution costs for the modes we choose across all activities must not exceed the project’s budget. This is a fixed cap that cannot be overrun.

What must be decided
- Choose one mode for each activity to balance speed, cost, and resource usage.
- Determine a feasible sequence for all pairs of activities that require ordering due to precedence, the minimum/maximum delay rules, and the conservative safety rule for resource conflicts.
- Set start times that honor release dates and ensure any activity with a hard deadline finishes on or before it.
- Coordinate these choices so that the overall project completes as early as possible without violating the budget or the rules above.

Why this is challenging
- Acceleration opportunities are constrained by the budget and by resource sharing; speeding one activity may force a delay elsewhere due to the safety rule.
- Maximum delay limits on certain dependencies reduce flexibility and may force earlier starts for some tasks, tightening the schedule.
- The combination of mode choices, sequencing decisions, and timing windows creates many interdependencies that must be evaluated together to identify a feasible and efficient plan.

Goal
Minimize the total project duration while staying within budget, respecting all precedence links and delay windows, honoring release dates and deadlines, and applying the resource safety rule described above.

Next steps
- Validate the data set in the annex.
- Run scenario analyses to compare feasible schedules under different mode selections within the budget.
- Identify activities where upgrading to faster modes yields the greatest reduction in overall completion time without triggering additional sequencing constraints.
- Confirm the final schedule and mode selections with workstream leads before baselining.
